newsitem.title: ITALY: Albania's Nano says will not repay lost savings.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Nano says will not repay lost savings.

text.p: Albania's new prime minister Fatos Nano said on Wednesday his government would not reimburse people who lost money in a massive savings scandal earlier this year, but hoped to compensate them with a revived economy.

"We will not reimburse, but we will give more than what they lost," Nano told reporters on the eve of an international donors' conference in Rome that will discuss how to rebuild Albania's shattered economy after months of unrest.
"We want to offer everyone mechanisms whereby they can save, invest and earn so they feel reimbursed for what they lost," Nano said after meeting Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

The collapse of shaky investment pyramid schemes earlier this year swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians, and triggered months of anarchy which led to the fall of the right-wing government of former President Sali Berisha.
Nano and his Socialist party, which crushed Berisha's Democratic Party in June elections, had campaigned on a pledge to do his utmost to repay savers.

Albania's parliament voted on Wednesday to audit the nation's surviving high-interest investment schemes and examine the defunct pyramid schemes in a bid to return at least some of the population's lost savings.
Nano said he was hoping to secure from Thursday's international conference, not only financial backing, but a commitment to help in development programmes in Albania, Europe's poorest economy.
"We do not want suitcases or floods of cash to Albania. We want to be able to create together development programmes that will go hand in hand with new jobs," he said.

Before leaving Tirana for Rome, Nano told reporters the Albanian delegation would "define the priorities of our work, the framework of talks with world institutions and ways of communicating with donors, banks and other governments...so that our programme can be applied immediately."
Thursday's meeting is a preparatory conference for a high-level donors' conference in October.
Prodi, who met Nano for more than two hours, reiterated Italy's commitment to continue supporting Albania's economic and political recovery.
"The first phase has finished. But now starts a second, perhaps more difficult phase, which is the reconstruction of the economy," Prodi said.
"Our commitment is for the immediate revival of the economic and political life of the country."
Italy led a 7,000-strong multinational security force which was deployed in April to help restore order and secure safe elections, and is expected to withdraw completely by August 12.
Prodi said Italy would send, upon the Albanian government's request, more soldiers, this time with civil duties, including helping to train Albanian military and police forces.
On Tuesday, parliament, dominated by the Socialist Party and its allies with 119 seats in the 155-seat chamber, gave resounding backing to Nano's policies to restore order.

The secretary-general of the opposition Democratic Party, Genc Pollo, said on Wednesday that Nano's programme would deepen the economic crisis and further impoverish the Albanian people, triggering disillusion and social upheaval.
